articles.excerpt: Linux permissions control how users access, modify, and execute files or directories on a system. Efficient management of user permissions improves system security and access control by preventing una…
articles.body: Linux permissions control how users access, modify, and execute files or directories on a system. Efficient management of user permissions improves system security and access control by preventing unauthorized access to sensitive data, files, and directories. This guide explains how to read and interpret Linux permissions, then use the chmod and chown commands to change them. By the end, you'll be able to view, calculate, and modify file and directory permissions — including special permissions like the sticky bit, SUID, and SGID — on your Linux workstation. Linux Permissions Linux permissions are categorized into read, write, and execute (RWX), which define user or group privileges on a file or directory: Read ( r ) : View the contents of a file or list the contents of a directory.

articles.title: Managing Node Applications with PM2
articles.excerpt: Node.js is an open-source JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine, known for its speed and scalability in real-time and high-performance applications. Running Node applications in production co…
articles.body: Node.js is an open-source JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine, known for its speed and scalability in real-time and high-performance applications. Running Node applications in production comes with unique challenges — you need to handle unexpected crashes, manage processes, and ensure continuous uptime. PM2 is a production process manager for Node.js applications that simplifies this, letting you monitor, restart, and optimize your apps. This guide walks through installing PM2, running a sample Node.js app under it, and configuring PM2 for production use. By the end, you'll have a Node.js application managed by PM2 with automatic restarts, centralized logs, and startup persistence configured.

articles.title: Viewing and Managing System Logs Using rsyslog in Linux
articles.excerpt: Linux systems generate a continuous stream of logs from the kernel, services, and user applications, and managing them is essential for diagnosing issues, tracking activity, and maintaining operationa…
articles.body: Linux systems generate a continuous stream of logs from the kernel, services, and user applications, and managing them is essential for diagnosing issues, tracking activity, and maintaining operational visibility. rsyslog is a widely adopted logging daemon that collects, processes, stores, and optionally forwards these logs, supporting multiple input sources, advanced filtering, rule-based message routing, and remote logging capabilities beyond what basic syslog tools offer. This guide uses rsyslog to view and manage system logs, define custom rules, and forward logs to remote servers for centralized logging. By the end, you'll have custom rsyslog rules routing SSH and application logs to their own files, plus a client forwarding logs to a centralized remote server.

articles.excerpt: nftables is a modern packet filtering framework for Linux that replaces iptables. It offers a unified and efficient way to manage firewall rules across multiple protocols like IPv4, IPv6, and ARP, wit…
articles.body: nftables is a modern packet filtering framework for Linux that replaces iptables. It offers a unified and efficient way to manage firewall rules across multiple protocols like IPv4, IPv6, and ARP, with better performance and a simpler configuration through a single interface instead of multiple tables. This guide installs and configures nftables on Linux, sets up basic firewall rules, manages network traffic, and implements common security policies. By the end, you'll have a persistent nftables firewall with SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS access rules, NAT/port forwarding, and logging in place. Prerequisites Before you begin, you need to: Have access to a Linux-based instance as a non-root sudo user. Have a basic understanding of network protocols and firewall rule management.

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.body: The Steam Frame came out a month ago, and while it's one of the best PCVR headsets out there, its lenses weren't quite as high-quality as some of its competitors. However, it seems like Valve might be working on a mid-generation refresh with OLED optics. According to SteamFrameHub , which dug through some of the source code for the Steam Frame kernel, the OS has references to a different Steam Frame with OLED optics, code named 'Plano.' Take this with a massive grain of salt, of course. But if it's real, the Plano headset would have largely the same specs as the existing Steam Frame, just with OLED panels with a per-eye resolution of 3,552x3,840, compared to the 2,160x2,160 pancake lenses found in the Steam Frame.

Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
